title: Open the right door
brief: Callers speak different languages: a chat UI, a webhook, a phone line, another agent, Teams. A hosted agent can expose several protocols, so decide who owns the conversation and which channel the callers use.

blocks.md: A hosted agent can expose several protocols at once [[r2]]. Choose by who owns the conversation and what the caller sends. The docs' default advice is to start with Responses and add Invocations later. Each hosted agent gets its own endpoint at deploy time, so programmatic callers need no publishing step. Publishing is for people in Teams or Microsoft 365 Copilot [[r5]].

blocks.title: Pick a protocol
blocks.prompt: Change the caller, the history owner and the channel.

ui.why: Any OpenAI-compatible SDK is the client.

hook.why: A webhook payload does not fit a conversation shape.

peer.why: Works as a tool call, but A2A models tasks.

own.why: You would fight the managed history.

teams.why: Activity is bridged from Responses on publish.

ui.why: Works, but you build what Responses gives.

hook.why: Built for webhooks, batch and custom streams.

voice.why: Request and response, not a socket.

peer.why: Possible, but not a peer contract.

own.why: Full control of sessions and SSE.

teams.why: Activity bridges from Responses, not Invocations.

ui.why: A chat UI does not need a socket.

voice.why: Real-time voice with Pipecat, LiveKit or Voice Live.

teams.why: A real-time audio socket is not a Teams chat path (inference).

peer.why: Built for agent to agent tasks.

none.why: Fits cross-team calls with no channel.

blocks.takeaway: Responses is the default and the only route to Teams. Leave it when the payload, the stream or the caller is not a conversation.

blocks.title: Publishing scope
blocks.intro: Publishing to Microsoft Copilot and Teams is GA as of 2026-10-13.

options.name: Individual scope
options.summary: Previously called Shared (`publishScope` Shared). No admin approval.
pros: Ships a pilot without waiting for approval
cons: Not listed under Built by your org
options.bestWhen: A pilot or a small group needs the agent this week.
options.avoidWhen: The whole organization needs a managed listing.

options.name: Organization scope
options.summary: `publishScope` Tenant. An admin approves it in the Microsoft 365 admin center, then it is listed under Built by your org.
options.bestWhen: The agent is production and widely used.
options.avoidWhen: You are still iterating on a prototype.

options.name: No publishing
options.summary: Call the agent's own endpoint programmatically.
cons: No Teams or Microsoft 365 Copilot presence
options.bestWhen: Callers are services, apps or other agents.
options.avoidWhen: People expect to chat with it in Teams.

items.symptom: A voice client reconnects and the assistant forgets the conversation
items.cause: Invocations (WebSocket) leaves session state to you (inference from the protocol rules)
items.fix: Persist state in `$HOME` or the key-value store, keyed by a session id the client resends.

items.cause: The agent waits for admin approval in the Microsoft 365 admin center
items.fix: Request the approval, and use Individual scope for the pilot meanwhile.

items.symptom: Publishing fails with an authorization error
items.cause: A missing role (Azure Bot Service Contributor, Contributor or Owner, plus Foundry User on the project) or an unregistered `Microsoft.BotService` provider
items.fix: Grant the roles and register the provider before you publish [[r5]].

items.symptom: A peer agent cannot call the endpoint
items.cause: The peer speaks a different A2A version. On hosted agents v1.0 is GA and v0.3 is preview
items.fix: Declare the version you serve and test the peer against it.

quiz.q: A billing system posts JSON events to the agent and expects its own streaming format. There is no Microsoft 365 channel and the caller keeps its own sessions. Which protocol fits?
quiz.explain: Invocations is for webhooks, batch work and custom streaming, and you manage sessions. Responses forces a conversation shape and platform-kept history. WebSocket is for real-time voice. A2A is a peer-agent task protocol, not a webhook receiver.

quiz.q: Match each caller to the protocol the docs point to.

pairs.l: Chat UI with platform-kept history and Teams publishing
Webhook or batch extraction with a custom payload
Real-time voice client with Voice Live in the container

quiz.explain: Responses keeps history and bridges to Activity for Teams. Invocations hands payload and sessions to you. The WebSocket variant carries real-time audio. A2A models tasks between peer agents.

quiz.q: A team wants a pilot in Teams this week and a managed listing for the whole company next quarter. Which sequence matches how the scopes work?
options: Organization scope first, because Individual scope needs a tenant-wide admin approval before anyone can use the agent in Teams
Individual scope for both phases, because Organization scope is reserved for Microsoft-built agents
Individual scope for the pilot, then Organization scope with admin approval and a Built by your org listing
No publishing at all, because the Activity protocol works without an Azure Bot Service resource
quiz.explain: Individual scope needs no admin approval, which suits a pilot. Organization scope (`publishScope` Tenant) needs approval in the Microsoft 365 admin center and then lists under Built by your org. Individual scope does not need tenant approval, Organization scope is not Microsoft-only, and publishing creates the Azure Bot Service resource that carries Activity.

takeaways: Start with Responses, add Invocations or WebSocket when the caller is not a chat
Only Responses bridges to Activity for Teams and Microsoft 365
Individual scope ships a pilot, Organization scope needs admin approval
A2A v1.0 is GA and v0.3 is preview on hosted agents, so state the version you serve
